flashcards.question: What is e-business?
flashcards.answer: The use of the Web, Internet, intranets or extranets to conduct business. It goes beyond simple online buying/selling to include wider business processes such as supply chain management, electronic order processing and customer relationship management (CRM).
flashcards.explanation: E-business runs the whole business electronically, not just sales.

flashcards.question: How does e-business differ from e-commerce?
flashcards.answer: E-commerce is the trading activity (buying and selling) carried out through electronic devices. E-business is broader — running the entire business through the internet (including SCM, CRM, ERP, order processing).
flashcards.explanation: E-commerce ⊂ e-business.

flashcards.question: What are the main components/areas of e-business?
flashcards.answer:
Key areas: E-Procurement, Online Stores, Online Marketplace, Online Communities, Online Companies.
(Plus BI, CRM, ERP, SCM, collaboration and electronic transactions.)
flashcards.explanation: These cover sourcing, selling, connecting and cooperating online.

flashcards.question: What is e-procurement?
flashcards.answer: Also called "supplier exchange" — sourcing products or services electronically (B2B, B2G, B2C) to reduce a company’s costs and effort.
flashcards.explanation: Buying side of e-business.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between an online store and an online marketplace?
flashcards.answer: An online store (e-shop, web-store, m-commerce) sells its OWN products/services via a website or app. An online marketplace connects buyers and suppliers — the operator only presents other people’s inventory and provides the transaction facility.
flashcards.explanation: Store = own goods; marketplace = others’ goods.

flashcards.question: What are online communities in e-business?
flashcards.answer: Groups of people with the same interests or purposes who use the internet to communicate, helping individuals and organizations make transaction decisions.
flashcards.explanation: Communities influence buying decisions.

flashcards.question: Who are the three market participants in e-business?
flashcards.answer: Business (B), Consumer/citizen (C) and Administration (A). Each can be a buyer or a provider, giving 9 possible relationship combinations.
flashcards.explanation: B, C and A combine into models like B2C, B2B, etc.

flashcards.question: Which relationships belong to e-commerce vs e-government?
flashcards.answer: B2C and B2B belong to e-commerce. A2B (administration-to-business) and A2A (administration-to-administration) belong to e-government — both are part of e-business.
flashcards.explanation: E-government is the public-administration side of e-business.

options: Using the Web/Internet to conduct the whole business

learn.content:
E-Business

E-business is the use of the Web, Internet, intranets and extranets to conduct business. Unlike e-commerce (just buying/selling online), it covers the whole business: supply chain management, order processing, CRM and more.

Main components

  • E-Procurement — sourcing goods/services electronically to cut costs.
  • Online Store — sells its own products (e-shop, m-commerce).
  • Online Marketplace — connects buyers & suppliers (others’ inventory).
  • Online Communities — interest groups that shape transaction decisions.
  • Online Companies — companies cooperating as a virtual business.

Market participants

Business (B), Consumer (C), Administration (A) — 9 combinations. B2C & B2B = e-commerce; A2B & A2A = e-government.

flashcards.question: What is digital transformation?
flashcards.answer: A change in the way an organization operates — its systems, processes, workflow and culture. It brings data together across areas and uses automation and AI/ML to connect the customer journey.
flashcards.explanation: "Digital or die" — it affects every level of the organization.

flashcards.question: Name the key digital technologies driving modern business.
flashcards.answer:
• Mobile technology (AR/VR)
• Cloud computing
• Social media
• Big Data & real-time analytics
• Sensors & IoT (Internet of Things)
• Artificial Intelligence (AI)
flashcards.explanation: These technologies enable digital transformation.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between ANI and AGI?
flashcards.answer: ANI (narrow AI) is programmed for a single task and is what is available today (e.g. Siri, Google Translate). AGI (general AI) can perform as well as or better than humans across a wide range of cognitive tasks.
flashcards.explanation: Today’s AI is narrow (ANI); AGI is still aspirational.

flashcards.question: How is recognition technology used in hotels?
flashcards.answer: Retina and fingerprint scanning to unlock hotel rooms (no key card to lose). In future, facial biometrics could automatically authorise payments or check guests out, reducing queues.
flashcards.explanation: Improves guest experience and security.

flashcards.question: How are robots used in tourism and travel?
flashcards.answer: To perform intelligent tasks — from customer service to data processing. Example: the Amadeus 1A-TA robot (powered by deep learning) acts as a digital assistant, analysing preferences and recommending destinations.
flashcards.explanation: Robots augment staff and personalise service.

flashcards.question: What is mobile integration in hospitality?
flashcards.answer: Using a hotel app for room bookings, restaurant/spa reservations and room service; beacon technology to send location-based promotions; and combining with IoT so guests control room appliances from their phone.
flashcards.explanation: The phone becomes the guest’s control centre.

flashcards.question: What is the Internet of Things (IoT)?
flashcards.answer: A network of sensors and connected devices. In hotels it lets guests control room appliances and enables data collection, often combined with mobile apps.
flashcards.explanation: Physical devices connected to the internet.

flashcards.question: Why is digital transformation important ("digital or die")?
flashcards.answer: It lets companies operate more effectively, connect the customer journey across data, and stay competitive — affecting every level of the organization.
flashcards.explanation: Falling behind digitally threatens the business.

learn.content:
IT Trends & Innovations in Modern Business

Digital transformation changes how an organization operates — systems, processes, workflow and culture — bringing data together and using automation + AI/ML to connect the customer journey ("digital or die").

Key digital technologies

Mobile (AR/VR), Cloud computing, Social media, Big Data & analytics, Sensors & IoT, and Artificial Intelligence.

AI: ANI vs AGI

ANI (narrow) does a single task (Siri, Google Translate). AGI (general) could match or beat humans across many cognitive tasks.

Trends in tourism & travel

  • Recognition technology — retina/fingerprint to unlock rooms; facial biometrics for payments/check-out.
  • Robots — customer service & data processing (e.g. Amadeus 1A-TA digital assistant).
  • Mobile integration + IoT — app bookings, beacons, and controlling room appliances from a phone.

flashcards.question: What are the three types of decisions in an organization?
flashcards.answer:
• Structured — well-defined standard procedure, can be automated ("programmable tasks")
• Semistructured — has a structured aspect that benefits from analytical models and IS technology
• Unstructured — one-time, no standard procedure; relies on the decision maker’s intuition (IT offers less support)
flashcards.explanation: Semistructured & unstructured involve multiple, often conflicting criteria.

flashcards.question: What is a Management Support System (MSS)?
flashcards.answer: Different types of information systems developed to support certain aspects and types of decisions — each designed with unique goals and objectives.
flashcards.explanation: MSS = umbrella for decision-supporting systems.

flashcards.question: What are the four phases of decision making?
flashcards.answer:
1. Intelligence — scan the environment, collect & process data
2. Design — define criteria and generate alternatives
3. Choice — select the best feasible alternative
4. Implementation — carry out the choice and assess performance
flashcards.explanation: Intelligence → Design → Choice → Implementation.

flashcards.question: What happens in the Intelligence phase?
flashcards.answer: The decision maker examines the organization’s environment for conditions that need decisions; data is collected from various sources and processed to discover ways to approach the problem.
flashcards.explanation: Finding the problem.

flashcards.question: What happens in the Design phase (and does IT support it)?
flashcards.answer: Defines criteria, generates alternatives and the associations between criteria and alternatives. Information technology does NOT support this phase.
flashcards.explanation: Creative phase — least IT support.

flashcards.question: What is a Decision Support System (DSS)?
flashcards.answer: A system that helps sort through possible solutions to choose the best one for the organization; it includes tools for calculating cost-benefit ratios and does follow-up assessment of how a solution performs.
flashcards.explanation: Supports the Choice and Implementation phases.

flashcards.question: Give a hospitality example of the decision-making phases (Marriott).
flashcards.answer: Intelligence: analyse guest feedback/market trends (reviews, surveys, social media). Design: develop initiatives (e.g. "Serve 360" sustainability, digital keys). Choice: evaluate costs/benefits/ROI (global vs per-hotel strategy). Implementation: roll out and assess.
flashcards.explanation: Each phase maps to a real management action.

learn.content:
Management Support Systems

Types of decisions

  • Structured — clear procedure, can be automated.
  • Semistructured — partly structured; benefits from analytical models.
  • Unstructured — one-time, no procedure; relies on intuition.

Four phases of decision making

Intelligence (find the problem, gather data) → Design (criteria + alternatives; IT does not support this) → Choice (pick the best; a DSS helps with cost-benefit) → Implementation (carry out + assess).

DSS = Decision Support System: sorts solutions and computes cost-benefit ratios.

flashcards.question: What is an expert system?
flashcards.answer: A computer system that emulates (acts in all respects with) the decision-making capabilities of a human expert (Prof. Edward Feigenbaum, Stanford).
flashcards.explanation: A branch of artificial intelligence.

flashcards.question: What are the two main components of an expert system?
flashcards.answer:
• Knowledge base — facts obtained from books, magazines, knowledgeable persons, etc.
• Inference engine — draws conclusions from the knowledge base
flashcards.explanation: Knowledge base = what it knows; inference engine = how it reasons.

flashcards.question: What does the inference engine do?
flashcards.answer: It draws conclusions from the knowledge base — applying the stored knowledge to reach decisions.
flashcards.explanation: The reasoning part of the system.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between problem domain and knowledge domain?
flashcards.answer: An expert’s knowledge is specific to one problem domain (medicine, finance, engineering…). The knowledge about solving specific problems is the knowledge domain. The problem domain is always a superset of the knowledge domain.
flashcards.explanation: Knowledge domain ⊂ problem domain.

flashcards.question: What are the advantages of expert systems?
flashcards.answer:
• Increased availability
• Reduced cost
• Reduced danger
• Performance
• Multiple expertise
• Increased reliability
flashcards.explanation: They make expert knowledge widely and cheaply available.

flashcards.question: What technology may an expert system include?
flashcards.answer: Special expert-system languages (e.g. CLIPS), programs, and hardware designed to facilitate their implementation.
flashcards.explanation: CLIPS is a classic expert-system language.

learn.content:
Knowledge-Based & Expert Systems

An expert system is a computer system that emulates the decision-making capabilities of a human expert (Edward Feigenbaum). It is a branch of artificial intelligence.

Main components

  • Knowledge base — facts from books, experts, etc.
  • Inference engine — draws conclusions from the knowledge base.

Domains & advantages

An expert’s knowledge is specific to one problem domain (medicine, finance…); the knowledge domain is a subset of it. Advantages: increased availability, reduced cost, reduced danger, performance, multiple expertise, increased reliability.

flashcards.question: What is information systems security?
flashcards.answer: The protection of information systems against unauthorized access to or modification of information (in storage, processing or transit), and against denial of service to authorized users — including measures to detect, document and counter such threats. (NIST)
flashcards.explanation: Protects confidentiality, integrity and availability.

flashcards.question: What is malware?
flashcards.answer: Malicious software — any program or code created to harm a computer, network or server. It is the most common type of cyberattack and includes ransomware, trojans, spyware, viruses, worms, keyloggers, bots and cryptojacking.
flashcards.explanation: Umbrella term for malicious code.

flashcards.question: What is ransomware?
flashcards.answer: Malware that denies legitimate users access to their system and demands a payment (ransom) — often in untraceable cryptocurrency. It blocks the hard drive or encrypts files; victims may not regain access even after paying.
flashcards.explanation: Exploits vulnerabilities to lock/encrypt data.

flashcards.question: What is a DoS / DDoS attack?
flashcards.answer: A Denial-of-Service attack floods a network with false requests to disrupt business operations, so users cannot perform routine tasks (email, websites, accounts). It costs time, money and resources to restore operations.
flashcards.explanation: Goal is disruption, not usually data theft.

flashcards.question: What is phishing?
flashcards.answer: A cyberattack that uses email, SMS, phone, social media and social-engineering techniques to entice a victim into sharing sensitive information such as passwords or account numbers.
flashcards.explanation: Relies on tricking the human, not the machine.

flashcards.question: How can an organization protect against cyber attacks?
flashcards.answer:
• Train staff
• Keep software and systems up to date
• Ensure endpoint protection
• Install a firewall
• Back up data
• Control access to systems
• Secure the Wi-Fi
flashcards.explanation: Layered defence: people + technology + process.

learn.content:
Information Systems Security

Information systems security is protecting information systems against unauthorized access or modification (in storage, processing or transit) and against denial of service to authorized users — including detecting, documenting and countering threats (NIST).

Most common cyber attacks

  • Malware — any malicious code (most common); includes the others below.
  • Ransomware — locks/encrypts data and demands a ransom (crypto).
  • DoS / DDoS — floods a network with false requests to disrupt operations.
  • Phishing — fake email/SMS + social engineering to steal credentials.
Protect: train staff, update software, endpoint protection, firewall, backups, access control, secure Wi-Fi.
